title: The Definite Integral and Its Properties
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: The definite integral ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx is the limit of Riemann sums and represents net signed area.
Net signed area means area above the x-axis counts positive and area below the x-axis counts negative.
When f(x) is negative, the rectangle heights are negative, so the integral subtracts that region's area.
The definite integral generally does not equal total geometric area, which counts all regions positively.
Example: ∫ from 0 to 2π of sin x dx = 0 because the positive arch cancels the negative arch, even though the total area is 4.
The constant multiple rule: ∫ from a to b of k·f(x) dx = k·∫ from a to b of f(x) dx.
The sum and difference rule: ∫ from a to b of [f(x) ± g(x)] dx = ∫ f dx ± ∫ g dx over the same interval.
Interval additivity: ∫ from a to b of f dx + ∫ from b to c of f dx = ∫ from a to c of f dx.
Reversing the limits flips the sign: ∫ from a to b of f dx = −∫ from b to a of f dx.
The zero-width rule: ∫ from a to a of f(x) dx = 0, since there is no interval to accumulate over.
The comparison property: if f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b], then ∫ from a to b of f dx ≥ ∫ from a to b of g dx.
A definite integral can be evaluated geometrically when the integrand graphs as a triangle, rectangle, or semicircle.
Example: ∫ from 0 to 4 of (1/2 x) dx is a right triangle of base 4 and height 2, giving area 4.
Example: ∫ from −2 to 2 of √(4 − x²) dx is a semicircle of radius 2, giving area 2π.
When a region lies partly below the axis, the definite integral is the net of positive and negative areas, while total area requires splitting at the x-intercepts and summing absolute values.
A common AP task gives integral values and asks for combinations using the properties, without any formula for f.
Example: if ∫ from 0 to 3 of f = 5 and ∫ from 3 to 7 of f = 2, then by additivity ∫ from 0 to 7 of f = 7.
Example: if ∫ from 1 to 4 of f = 8 and ∫ from 1 to 6 of f = 3, then ∫ from 4 to 6 of f = 3 − 8 = −5.
The order of the limits is the most common source of sign errors; a swapped interval negates the integral.
If v(t) is velocity, ∫ from a to b of v(t) dt is the displacement (net change in position), with direction handled by the sign.
Total distance traveled requires integrating speed |v(t)|, which makes every contribution positive.
The integral of a rate of change over an interval equals the net change in the underlying quantity, the seed of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
